input.question: How was knowledge ‘lost’ after the fall of Rome?
input.ground_truth: In addition to the excellent answers we've got here, in [this thread](_URL_0_), /u/Tiako and /u/bitparity discuss quality of life after the fall of the Roman Empire, which, will not a strict answer to OP's question, certainly has a lot of overlap and will probably prove to be of interest.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

I am a man.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How was knowledge ‘lost’ after the fall of Rome?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big box of toys. You know how to play with all of them and you tell your friends how to play too. But one day, something bad happens and you can’t play with your toys anymore. The toys are still there, but you and your friends forget how to play with them the right way. Some toys get broken or lost. Some new people come and they don’t know the old games, so they make up new ones.

That’s kind of what happened after the fall of Rome. Rome was like a big, smart city with lots of books and knowledge—like a giant toy box. People in Rome knew lots of things about math, building, medicine, and stories. But when Rome fell, there was a lot of fighting and changing leaders. Many of the books and smart people left or were lost. Not as many people could read or write anymore. So, for a while, people forgot or didn’t know a lot of the old smart things.

It wasn’t that the knowledge just disappeared, but it became hard to find and remember, like forgetting how to play with your toys until someone finds the old rule book again.
